reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / relevant specialty textbook
clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous DNA-repair disorder, usually autosomal recessive (with rare X-linked and dominant forms), caused by variants in one of many FANC pathway genes that repair DNA interstrand crosslinks
Progressive bone marrow failure typically emerges in the first decade, presenting with cytopenias and often preceded by macrocytosis and thrombocytopenia
Congenital anomalies are common but variable, including short stature, radial-ray and thumb defects, cafe-au-lait macules, renal anomalies and microphthalmia
There is a very high risk of myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia, and of solid tumours, notably head and neck and gynaecological squamous cell carcinomas at young ages
The diagnostic test is a chromosomal breakage study showing excessive chromosomal breakage after exposure to DNA crosslinking agents such as diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C
Somatic mosaicism from reversion in haematopoietic cells can cause false-negative blood breakage tests, so fibroblast testing may be needed
Extreme sensitivity to radiation and crosslinking chemotherapy demands markedly modified conditioning and treatment protocols
reference.pathophysiology: Fanconi anaemia results from biallelic (or, in the X-linked form, hemizygous) variants in any of numerous genes that cooperate in the Fanconi anaemia/BRCA DNA-repair pathway, which recognises and repairs DNA interstrand crosslinks and helps maintain genomic stability during replication. Failure of this pathway leaves cells unable to resolve crosslink damage, producing chromosomal breakage and instability that drives progressive haematopoietic stem cell attrition (bone marrow failure) and a strong predisposition to leukaemia and squamous carcinomas. The same defect underlies the hypersensitivity of cells to crosslinking agents, which is exploited in the diagnostic breakage assay.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (dyskeratosis congenita, Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome)
Bloom syndrome and Nijmegen breakage syndrome
VACTERL association without an underlying repair defect
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal breakage analysis with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C as the diagnostic test
Fibroblast (skin) breakage testing when blood results are equivocal owing to somatic mosaicism
Molecular genetic testing to identify the causative FANC gene and complementation group
Full blood count and bone marrow examination with cytogenetics to assess marrow failure and clonal evolution
Regular head and neck and gynaecological examination for early squamous malignancy
Renal and skeletal imaging and endocrine assessment for associated anomalies
redFlags: Rapidly falling blood counts or new blasts suggesting evolution to myelodysplastic syndrome or acute leukaemia
A new head and neck or anogenital mucosal lesion raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma
Severe unexpected toxicity from standard-dose radiotherapy or chemotherapy
Signs of severe marrow failure such as life-threatening bleeding or infection
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is guarded and dominated by progressive bone marrow failure and a lifelong, cumulative risk of leukaemia and early-onset solid cancers. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can address marrow failure but does not remove and may increase the risk of later solid tumours, so cancer surveillance must continue lifelong.
pitfalls: Accepting a normal blood breakage test in a suspicious case without pursuing fibroblast testing for mosaicism
Administering standard conditioning or chemotherapy doses, causing severe toxicity from the underlying repair defect
Attributing isolated congenital anomalies to another syndrome and delaying diagnosis
Relaxing cancer surveillance after transplantation despite the continuing solid-tumour risk
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Refer for allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation to correct bone marrow failure, the definitive treatment for the marrow disease
Support cytopenias with androgens such as oxymetholone and with blood product transfusion while monitoring for complications
Minimise DNA-damaging exposures and drastically reduce chemotherapy and radiotherapy dosing given crosslinker hypersensitivity
Maintain intensive lifelong surveillance for myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukaemia and early-onset head-and-neck and gynaecological squamous carcinomas
Promote risk reduction through tobacco and alcohol avoidance and HPV vaccination
Provide genetic counselling, identify the causative FANC gene and complementation group, and offer cascade testing of relatives
Coordinate multidisciplinary care for associated renal, skeletal and endocrine anomalies
